set.explanation: Syncope during exertion in a young person is a red flag for structural heart disease, above all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (dynamic LV outflow obstruction and ventricular arrhythmias), and also aortic stenosis or anomalous coronary arteries; echocardiography is the key test. A normal resting ECG does not exclude these. Carotid sinus massage is for suspected carotid sinus hypersensitivity in older people, and a head CT or glucose level is unhelpful after a brief faint with rapid, complete recovery. The patient should avoid competitive sport until serious causes are excluded (ECG, echo, ambulatory monitoring and, if needed, cardiac MRI).

why: Same question as 39 Blocks cvsx-0001 (young man with exertional syncope and normal ECG: echocardiogram)
Same idea as 39 Blocks arr-0015 (recognised causes of a prolonged PR interval, EXCEPT question)
Same question as 39 Blocks pleura-0004 (causes of empyema EXCEPT rheumatic fever); also misfiled in cardiology

set.explanation: Basic life support means maintaining airway, breathing and circulation without equipment: recognising the arrest, calling for help, and giving chest compressions with rescue breaths (30:2), plus early use of an automated external defibrillator where one is available. Intravenous drugs and manual defibrillation belong to advanced life support. ABCDE (adding disability and exposure) is the structured assessment of a deteriorating patient who still has a pulse, not a description of BLS.

why: BLS is support of airway, breathing and circulation (ABC); ABCDE is the assessment of the acutely ill patient, not resuscitation of an arrest

set.explanation: PEA is a non-shockable rhythm managed with high-quality CPR, adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as access is obtained (then every 3–5 minutes) and a search for reversible causes: the 4 Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and other metabolic disorders, hypothermia) and 4 Ts (thrombosis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins). Rhythm checks are every 2 minutes, not 1. Defibrillation and amiodarone are for VF or pulseless VT and do not restore output in PEA.

Atrial myxoma is a benign tumour, about 75% arising in the left atrium from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. It can prolapse through and obstruct the mitral valve (not the aortic valve), embolise (stroke, limb ischaemia) and cause constitutional symptoms with a raised ESR through interleukin-6 release. Although benign, it should be surgically excised promptly because of the risk of embolism and sudden obstruction; recurrence is uncommon except in familial forms such as Carney complex.

Primary cardiac tumours are rare (secondary deposits are far commoner), and among primary tumours in adults the myxoma is the most common, typically a pedunculated left atrial mass attached to the interatrial septum. Papillary fibroelastomas are small and arise on valve leaflets, fibromas and rhabdomyomas occur mainly in children within the ventricles, and angiosarcoma, the commonest primary malignant cardiac tumour, usually arises in the right atrium. An incidental left atrial mass is therefore most likely a myxoma and should be referred for surgical removal.

set.stem: A country with a population and environment very similar to China is moving from the first stage of the epidemiological transition ('pestilence and famine') to the second ('receding pandemics'). Regarding the expected pattern of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in this country, which of the following is true?
set.explanation: As countries move through the epidemiological transition, deaths from infection and malnutrition fall and CVD rises, first as rheumatic and infective heart disease, then hypertensive heart disease and haemorrhagic stroke, and later coronary heart disease. In China and similar East Asian populations, stroke mortality exceeds coronary mortality when CVD peaks, reflecting high rates of hypertension and salt intake. Countries do not follow the stages identically, patterns vary within a country (urban versus rural), and CVD mortality eventually falls in the later stages with prevention and treatment.

set.stem: A 67-year-old man complains of exertional breathlessness, leg oedema and waking at night acutely short of breath. You assess his volume status by examining the jugular venous pulse (JVP). Which of the following statements about JVP measurement is true?
set.explanation: The internal jugular vein reflects right atrial pressure, and the right atrium lies about 5 cm below the sternal angle in any position; with the patient sitting upright, the clavicle is well above this, so visible venous pulsation above the clavicle means a raised venous pressure. The measured height depends on the angle of inclination (usually 45°), and adding 5 cm to the height above the sternal angle gives only an estimate of central venous pressure. Normally the JVP falls with inspiration (a paradoxical rise is Kussmaul's sign), and the internal jugular is preferred because the external jugular has valves and is affected by local factors.

options: Systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases when measured in more distal arteries
Systolic leg blood pressures are usually as much as 20 mmHg lower than arm blood pressures
The concept of 'white coat hypertension' (pressures measured in clinical settings significantly higher than elsewhere) has been shown to be a myth
An inter-arm systolic difference of 25 mmHg is within normal limits
Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small results in a marked underestimation of the true blood pressure
set.explanation: Because of pulse-wave reflection and amplification, systolic pressure rises and diastolic pressure falls as the pulse travels to more distal arteries, so leg systolic pressure is normally higher than arm pressure (the basis of the ankle–brachial index). An inter-arm systolic difference above 10–15 mmHg is abnormal and suggests subclavian stenosis, aortic dissection or coarctation. A cuff that is too small overestimates blood pressure, and white coat hypertension is well recognised, which is why ambulatory or home monitoring is used to confirm the diagnosis.

why: Original option D (inter-arm difference under 20 mmHg) was arguably true; replaced with a clearly false statement

set.explanation: The impulse begins in the sinoatrial node, spreads through the atrial myocardium to the atrioventricular node, then down the His bundle, the bundle branches and Purkinje fibres to the ventricular myocardium. Automaticity is not unique to the SA node: AV-nodal and Purkinje cells also depolarise spontaneously but more slowly, providing escape rhythms. It is the left bundle branch that divides into anterior and posterior fascicles, and ventricular depolarisation spreads from endocardium to epicardium.

options: PR interval – conduction from the atria through the AV node and His–Purkinje system
set.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation; atrial repolarisation (the Ta wave) is small and usually hidden within the PR segment and QRS complex. The PR interval is the time from the start of atrial depolarisation to the start of ventricular depolarisation, most of it spent in the AV node. The QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation, the T wave ventricular repolarisation, and the U wave is thought to reflect late repolarisation (e.g. of Purkinje fibres), becoming prominent in hypokalaemia.

why: Original option B (PR interval – atrial repolarisation) was also an incorrect pairing, giving two answers; option rewritten

set.explanation: The normal frontal-plane QRS axis lies between −30° and +90° (some texts use +100° or +110°), so −20° is normal. Left axis deviation is −30° to −90° (so both −35° and −80° are left axis deviation, commonly from left anterior fascicular block or inferior MI), right axis deviation is beyond +90°, and −90° to ±180° is extreme (north-west) axis, seen in ventricular tachycardia or hyperkalaemia.

set.stem: What is the primary finding on the ECG shown?
set.explanation: The tracing shows sinus rhythm at about 70–75 beats/min with a normal axis, normal PR, QRS and QT intervals, normal R-wave progression across the chest leads and no ST-segment shift. The T waves are upright but not tall or tented relative to the QRS, so hyperkalaemia is not suggested, and QRS voltages do not meet LVH criteria. Recognising a normal ECG systematically (rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology) is the baseline for identifying abnormal ones.

why: Same Harrison scenario and question as cvsx-0019 (dialysis patient who missed dialysis during a snowstorm, ECG, which electrolyte abnormality: hyperkalaemia)

set.explanation: Pacemaker cells have no stable resting potential: during phase 4 the 'funny' current (If, through HCN channels) and calcium currents cause slow spontaneous depolarisation. The SA node does this faster than the AV node (40–60/min) or Purkinje fibres (20–40/min), so it reaches threshold first and overdrives the other pacemakers. Its phase 0 upstroke is actually slow (calcium-mediated), its anatomical location is not what makes it dominant, and other tissues also have automaticity.

set.stem: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes mellitus and osteoporosis is brought to the emergency department after a fall at home, followed immediately by intense left hip pain. She was found by a neighbour after several hours and cannot remember whether she lost consciousness. She is exquisitely tender over the left hip, and the leg is shortened and externally rotated. Her mucous membranes are dry and skin turgor is reduced. Blood pressure is 170/80 mmHg and heart rate 130 beats/min. Her rhythm strip is shown (arrows mark P waves). What is the most appropriate first step for her tachycardia?
set.explanation: The strip shows an atrial tachycardia with visible P waves of varying shape (arrows) before each QRS, consistent with multifocal atrial tachycardia (or sinus tachycardia), which in a patient with COPD is driven by the underlying stress: pain from a fractured neck of femur, dehydration after a long lie and possibly hypoxia. Treatment is of the cause: analgesia, IV fluids and oxygen as needed, and the rate will settle. Adenosine and DC cardioversion are for re-entrant SVT or unstable arrhythmias and do not help an automatic atrial rhythm, and digoxin or IV beta-blockers are inappropriate first steps (beta-blockers are also relatively risky in COPD and hypovolaemia).

set.stem: After a snowstorm has kept people indoors for 4 days, a middle-aged woman is brought to the emergency department obtunded. Her neighbours had not seen her since the snow started, and the police found her unconscious on the floor. A radial pulse is barely palpable and blood pressure is 60 mmHg systolic. She has an arteriovenous dialysis fistula in the left arm. Her ECG is shown. What electrolyte abnormality do you expect?
set.explanation: A dialysis-dependent patient who has missed several sessions is at high risk of severe hyperkalaemia, and the ECG shows a very wide, bizarre sine-wave pattern, the pre-terminal stage that follows peaked T waves, loss of P waves and QRS widening, and precedes VF or asystole. Treatment is immediate IV calcium (gluconate or chloride) to stabilise the myocardium, insulin with glucose and nebulised salbutamol to shift potassium into cells, then urgent dialysis. Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypercalcaemia do not produce this pattern (hypercalcaemia shortens the QT).

options: The denervated donor heart lacks resting vagal tone and responds only to circulating catecholamines
The transplant procedure permanently damages the SA node
set.explanation: The transplanted heart is denervated, so without resting vagal tone its SA node fires at its intrinsic rate of about 90–110 beats/min, producing a mild resting tachycardia. With exercise the rate rises slowly, driven by circulating catecholamines rather than sympathetic nerves, and it falls slowly afterwards. This is expected physiology rather than rejection or SA-node injury; atropine is ineffective in the denervated heart because it acts through vagal blockade.

why: Source key (SA-node damage) contradicted its own explanation; resting tachycardia after transplant is due to denervation
Same idea as cvsx-0036 (donor heart allocation is regional because of the limited cold ischaemic time); this copy was also mis-keyed

set.stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with breathlessness on exertion. He had an orthotopic heart transplant for non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy 5 years ago and has done well apart from one cytomegalovirus reactivation in the first year. For the past 3 months, he has become limited by breathlessness on progressively less exertion. He is adamant that he has no chest pain or pressure. He takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose prednisolone and is fully adherent. Echocardiography shows normal LV function and wall thickness, and his resting ECG shows sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
set.explanation: Cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a diffuse concentric intimal proliferation of the coronary arteries of the graft, is the main cause of late graft failure and death after the first year, and CMV infection is a risk factor. Because the heart is denervated, ischaemia rarely causes angina and presents instead with breathlessness, heart failure, arrhythmia or sudden death. Rejection usually causes LV dysfunction or wall thickening on echo and is commonest in the first year; the diagnosis is made by coronary angiography with intravascular imaging, and treatment includes statins, switching to an mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus or everolimus) and, in advanced cases, retransplantation.

set.stem: A 19-year-old woman attending a travel clinic complains of a painless swelling of one leg. The skin is thickened with a woody texture, and a bedside ultrasound shows patent veins without thrombus. You suspect lymphoedema due to the most common cause of secondary lymphoedema worldwide. What cause do you suspect?
set.explanation: Worldwide, the commonest cause of secondary lymphoedema is lymphatic filariasis, caused by Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia species transmitted by mosquitoes, which damage lymphatics and can produce elephantiasis. In high-income countries, cancer and its treatment (lymph node dissection or radiotherapy) is the commonest cause. Recurrent cellulitis or lymphangitis, lymphogranuloma venereum and tuberculosis are recognised but much less frequent causes.

set.stem: A woman has chronic lymphoedema of the leg following recurrent streptococcal lymphangitis in childhood. She finds the swelling unsightly and asks about treatment. All of the following are reasonable treatments for chronic lymphoedema EXCEPT:
set.explanation: Lymphoedema is a protein-rich interstitial fluid collection due to failed lymphatic drainage, so diuretics do not help and risk intravascular volume depletion and electrolyte disturbance. Management is complex decongestive therapy (manual lymphatic drainage, multilayer bandaging and then graduated compression garments), skin care to prevent cellulitis, exercise and limb elevation, with intermittent pneumatic compression as an adjunct. Liposuction or lymphatic surgery (lymphovenous anastomosis, lymph node transfer) is used in selected patients.

set.stem: While on call, you are bleeped to see a man who has had a massive rectal bleed. He is drowsy, with a blood pressure of 65/40 mmHg and a pulse of 130 beats/min. While IV access is obtained, he arrests and CPR is started. The monitor shows organised QRS complexes, but there is no pulse. CPR continues and adrenaline 1 mg IV has just been given. What is the most important next step in management?
options: Rapid IV infusion of blood products via the major haemorrhage protocol
set.explanation: This is PEA caused by hypovolaemia from massive haemorrhage, and the arrest will not be reversed unless circulating volume is restored, so blood products (with crystalloid only as a bridge) are given rapidly through large-bore access while CPR continues and the source of bleeding is addressed. PEA is non-shockable, so defibrillation and amiodarone are not indicated. Adrenaline is repeated every 3–5 minutes, not immediately, and atropine is no longer part of the arrest algorithm.

why: Original stem left adrenaline and volume replacement both defensible, and colloid is no longer recommended; stem now states adrenaline has been given and the volume option specifies blood products

set.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with chest pain of several days' duration. The pain is sharp and stabbing, located at the left sternal border, and worsened by coughing and by palpation. She has no family history of heart disease and no diabetes, hypertension, smoking or hyperlipidaemia. Physical examination, ECG and chest X-ray are all normal. Which further investigation is indicated?
set.explanation: Sharp, localised pain reproduced by palpation and worsened by coughing, in a woman with no risk factors and a normal examination, ECG and chest X-ray, is musculoskeletal chest wall pain (costochondritis) with a very low probability of coronary disease. Further cardiac testing is not indicated because the pre-test probability is too low for any test to be useful, and false-positive results would lead to unnecessary invasive procedures. Treatment is reassurance and simple analgesia such as an NSAID.
